Yesterday we learned that a judge allowed a $32 billion lawsuit to proceed alleging that Apple's face recognition feature in Apple Photos violates state privacy laws.

Despite the two companies having very different approaches to privacy, this case has been conflated with Meta's use of face recognition. The judge allowing the case to proceed fundamentally misunderstands how the feature works……

The prior allegations against Meta

To properly understand this situation, we need to start with a face recognition lawsuit against Meta dating back to 2015.

Because that face recognition was performed on Meta's servers, and Meta was able to identify those faces, the company did indeed break the law, and the case had merit, ultimately settling for $650 million.

Apple is now being sued under that same Illinois law — the Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA) — which prohibits companies from collecting biometric data without consent.

Apple's approach is very different

There is a major problem with this allegation: Apple absolutely does not collect biometric data when doing face recognition within the Apple Photos app. As Apple noted in a 2021 machine learning research paper, the recognition algorithm runs entirely on-device.

Additionally, all the iPhone does is tell you 'these photos might be the same person' — it doesn't actually know who that person is. Only the iPhone user themselves is able to attach a name to those faces.

Apple Photos' privacy policy reflects this as well.

I'm shocked that this lawsuit has been allowed to languish in the justice system for six years; just a few minutes of research would reveal that the allegations in the lawsuit are clearly wrong.

The courts and legislators should be applauding Apple for this approach to privacy, not conflating it with the privacy-invading approaches of companies like Meta.

This is yet another example of courts and legislators not understanding the technology they are trying to regulate. The most obvious example, of course, involves end-to-end encryption — multiple countries have threatened or tried to ban end-to-end encryption without any understanding of how it actually works.

Of course, I understand that judges and politicians cannot be experts in every area they need to deal with. But they have access to experts, and I'm astounded that these lawsuits and draft bills can get this far without anyone pointing out these fundamental flaws.
